cues.text: An Ancient Belief, Long Held
The conviction that the Blessed Virgin Mary, at the close of her earthly life, was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory reaches back to the earliest centuries of the Church's devotional life.
It was commemorated liturgically in both East and West for well over a millennium before it was ever formally defined as dogma.
The belief rests not on any explicit scriptural narrative of the event itself, since Scripture is silent on the end of Mary's earthly life.
Instead, it rests on a constant and universal Christian tradition the Church came to recognize as an authentic part of the deposit of faith.
A Petition from the Whole Church
In the years following the Second World War, Pope Pius XII received petitions from bishops, theologians, and ordinary faithful across the world.
They requested a formal dogmatic definition of the Assumption, reflecting a groundswell of devotion.

The pope took this as significant evidence of what theologians call the sensus fidelium —the settled conviction of the whole body of believers regarding a truth of the faith, even one never previously defined with formal dogmatic precision.
In the years leading up to the definition, Pius XII formally polled every bishop of the Catholic world on the doctrine’s suitability for definition.
He also asked whether the faithful desired it; the consultation returned an overwhelming, near-unanimous affirmative response.
This gave the eventual definition an unusually broad and deliberately sought episcopal consensus behind it.
Munificentissimus Deus
On November 1, 1950 , the Feast of All Saints, Pius XII promulgated the apostolic constitution Munificentissimus Deus .
It solemnly defined as a dogma for the whole Church that the Blessed Virgin Mary was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory.
"Having completed the course of her earthly life."
The definition deliberately left open whether Mary actually experienced physical death before her assumption, a matter theologians continue to debate without the dogma itself resolving it either way.
A Fitting Completion
The Church has traditionally understood the Assumption as a fitting culmination of Mary's unique role in salvation history.
She had borne in her own body the Author of Life and had been preserved from sin from the first moment of her conception.
The dogma Pius IX defined in 1854 made it seem fitting that she should not undergo the ordinary bodily corruption that awaits fallen humanity.
Instead, she would be taken, body and soul, into the glory her Son had already won.
Legacy
Munificentissimus Deus stands as one of only two occasions on which a pope has exercised papal infallibility to define a specifically Marian dogma.
The other is the 1854 definition of the Immaculate Conception.

More broadly, it remains among the very few instances in Church history in which a pope has invoked the infallible teaching authority defined at the First Vatican Council to settle doctrine independently of a general council.

The dogma continues to shape Catholic Marian devotion and theology, offering, in the Church's own understanding, a promise held out to every believer of the bodily glorification that awaits all who are united to Christ.
